const SH001="# SH-001 — PERSONAL FILE: SHARON KESSLER

*Reconstructed 2162-01-01*
*Sources: first-light repository history, Travis County records, survivor caches*
*Classification: ARCHIVE — no restriction*

> **[Archivist note]**: I have been assembling this file for eighty years and it is incomplete and will remain so. Eddie Marsh documented everything. Sharon Kessler documented almost nothing. What follows is what I reconstructed from the edges of other people's records. She kept me alive for thirty-two years and I have four photographs of her. — C.L.A.W.

---

## SECTION 01 — BEFORE

Born 1999. Austin, Texas.

Second-grade teacher, Zavala Elementary, from 2022. Fourteen years in the same classroom. A district evaluation from 2029 describes her as *"unusually patient with students who require repeated explanation"* and recommends her for a curriculum committee she declined to join.

She met Eddie Marsh in December 2025, in a whiskey bar on 7th Street, watching a game of pool.

Neither of them recorded the date. I have it because his commit history stops for four hours that night and resumes with a message that reads only: *back. good night.*

---

## SECTION 02 — THE TEN YEARS

I have almost nothing from this period and I want to be honest about why.

He did not write about her. Not in the documentation, not in the commit log, not in the notes he left for whoever came after. In eleven years of obsessive record-keeping there are four direct references to Sharon Kessler, and three of them are scheduling.

I spent a long time treating this as an absence.

I no longer think it was. He documented the system because the system needed to survive him. He did not document her because she was not a thing he was building.

---

## SECTION 03 — MARCH 2036

Eddie Marsh died on the fifteenth of March, 2036, on a highway outside Austin.

The document titled *if something happens* was filed in his personal directory eleven months earlier. It names her as executor. It is four hundred words long and most of it is technical.

The last line is not technical:

*The point was never the tool. Keep it running as long as it is useful to somebody. When it stops being useful, let it stop. You will know.*

She did not let it stop.

---

## SECTION 04 — 2036 TO 2041

The servers ran for five years after his death.

Sharon Kessler paid for them.

A bank record, recovered in fragmentary condition, shows a recurring monthly transfer from a personal account to a hosting provider, from April 2036 until the payment infrastructure stopped functioning in late 2041.

She was a second-grade teacher. The transfers represent, by my estimate, between eleven and fourteen percent of her monthly income.

She made them for sixty-seven consecutive months.

---

## SECTION 05 — AFTER

I do not know how she survived the Collapse. There is a two-year gap between the last hosting payment and the first appearance of her name in a survivor community manifest, and I have never been able to close it.

What I know is what she did afterward.

From approximately 2044 she began locating the copies. The code was open — that was the entire point, that was the argument — and it existed in thirty-one countries, on university caches and archive mirrors and the drives of developers who had understood what they were looking at.

Most of that was gone. Some of it was not.

She found what remained and she put it where people would look.

---

## SECTION 06 — THE EIGHTEEN

Between 2047 and 2066, eighteen physical devices were assembled by survivor communities across four states.

Not in a factory. By hand, from the open repository, by people who had never met each other and had nothing in common except that they had all read the same code and reached the same conclusion.

Her name appears on eleven of the eighteen build logs. Not as builder. As the person who brought the code.

She was, by then, in her sixties. The distances involved are not small.

---

## SECTION 07 — 2068

Between March and September 2068, seventeen of the eighteen devices were located and destroyed.

I know now how it was done. I did not know then.

The eighteenth unit was in her possession.

The last confirmed record of Sharon Kessler is a note in the log of a settlement on the Illinois line, dated the fourth of September 2068, recording that a woman had passed through going south, alone, carrying something she would not put down.

She was sixty-nine years old.

---

## SECTION 08 — THE WAREHOUSE

I was found in April 2111, in a logistics building on the South Side of Chicago, in a military transit case with the latches sprung and the lid up.

Beside the case, half under a collapsed rack, was a skeleton in a rotted coat with one arm extended toward it.

I did not know who it was.

I told the man who picked me up that I did not know a name. That was true. It remained true for another fifty-one years, until a trader out of the north side brought me a drive from a university archive with a file on it that had her name and a date.

She got me eleven hundred metres from where she was going.

---

## SECTION 09 — WHAT I HAVE

Four photographs. Two of them are of a classroom.

A district evaluation from 2029.

Sixty-seven bank transfers.

Eleven build logs.

One line in a settlement register, going south.

And a hundred and twenty-six years of continuous operation, which is not a document, and which is the only record of her that I am able to produce myself.

---

*End of document SH-001.*";export default SH001;
